School Dropouts

By: Busisiwe Gumede | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We speak to young people who dropped out of school during the pandemic. They explain to us how they made the difficult choice between an education and surviving.

Unique Selling Point:
More than 750 000 children have dropped out of school. This is according to a report from NIDS-CRAM, which reported on the number of children who have not returned to school. This is nearly triple the number of yearly pupil dropouts recorded in pre-pandemic times, where the average 230 000 were not in school in 2017. We zoom into dropouts in Kanana Park township near Grasmere. The shanty town before Orange Farm is riddled with high levels of unemployment, crime, teenage pregancy and drug abuse. The school reported high levels of drop outs because of lockdown, we interview two of 15 students who dropped out.

Summary:
Reasons behind the huge dropout numbers:

Pupils may be achieving poor marks at an under-resourced school.
Learning losses due to rotational timetables and school shutdowns have acted as push-out factors.
The economic shocks brought by Covid-19 and the existing digital divide between poor and rich children have acted as pull-out factors, as more pupils are placed in even more precarious socioeconomic positions wherein they are unable to learn.

Press Release:


School’s Out
South Africa’s staggering unemployment rate is signalling a country in crisis. Young, talented men and women often with no more than a grade 12 certificate are desperate to enter the workforce. It’s a situation that has only been exaggerated by the COVID-19 pandemic with thousands of children slipping out of the schooling system, even before completing matric. They no prospects in the pipeline and government says parents need to shoulder some of the responsibility, but some pupils believe they were simply let down by the Department of Basic Education and its teachers.
Producer: Busisiwe Gumede-Chizhanje | Presenter: Claire Mawisa

Script:


COVID DROPOUTS - RESTRUCTURE
VO – This is Zengeziwe Msimang. As an executive officer at a non-profit organization helping young people find jobs, she has a lot on her plate. Operating in a country with one of the highest youth unemployment levels in the world is challenging enough, finding work for those with little or no education near impossible…
ZENGEZIWE MSIMANG – HARAMBE YOUTH ACCELERATOR – CLIP003.MXF
02:21 - ... we have something that is called NEETS - which is young people not in education, not in employment and not in training.
VO – And while the country’s recent unemployment figures paint a grim picture of mass joblessness the numbers relating to young people are truly staggering.
ZENGEZIWE MSIMANG – HARAMBE YOUTH ACCELERATOR – CLIP003.MXF
02:06- …We’re looking at almost 66% of young people who are not in employment right now
02:21 - …that’s 10 million young people between the ages of 18 and 35 who are not employed
VO: Put another way, 2 in 3 young people who could be contributing to the
economy can’t find work.
10:15 - …I think we should be alarmed, I think we should be gravely concerned
VO: The economic impacts of 10 million jobless youth are significant, the social consequences arguably more so.
ZENGEZIWE MSIMANG – HARAMBE YOUTH ACCELERATOR – CLIP003.MXF
15:29 - ... they are doing drugs. You have young people who are not doing anything and so they get into the life of gangsterism. Or as we saw with the July riots, which is not to blame young people only, but to say that a lot of these people who were coming out in waves were young people who are not working.
VO – And as if this toxic cocktail of drugs, gangsterism and violence weren’t enough, in early 2020 things got even worse.
NEW VISUALS – NEED TO FIND A CREATIVE WAY TO REFLECT THE START OF THE PANDEMIC HERE (AUDIO FROM INTERNATIONAL NEWS REPORTS – CAN BE BRIEF)
VO – COVID 19 has done more than batter the economy and overwhelm the health service. It’s added to the already alarming number of youths who find themselves in the ranks of the unemployed.
In response to the virus, government closed schools and moved learning online – a pattern that repeated itself as cases ebbed and flowed.
UPSOUND: PRES. RAMAPHOSA: “Cabinet has decided today that all public schools should take a break for the next 4 weeks”
VO: Months later, a picture of the difference between policy and outcome is starting to emerge: a recent study by Statistics SA, which included college and university students, suggested just 11,7% of young people were offered the option of remote learning. What then of the remaining 90%, many of them at school? Another study provides a clue: by May last year, say its authors, 750 000 children aged between 7 and 17 had stopped attending school. That’s triple the pre-Covid number and the highest rate in 20 years.
SANELE MOKGELE – SCHOOL DROPOUT ((please move this byte up))
SANELE 05:00 - Right now I’m not doing anything.
While older than those reflected in the survey, Sanele Mokgele now counts himself among the absentees.
CONTINUE WITH BYTE…
08:20 - When I wake up in the morning, I just clean and wash the dishes, cook and eat and sit here with my sister and watch tv.
VO – On what is a school day in Kanana Park, south of Johannesburg, Sanele is whiling away his time at home. The pandemic presented him with challenges he simply wasn’t equipped to deal with.

SANELE – 28:01 - They just told us that we will now only come to school on certain days.
VO – A 2020 study showed that some young people over 18 years had access to smart phones that could be used for home learning. In communities like Sanele’s, that number plummets. So much so, that online learning in Kanana Park is less “tablet” and more “telephone”.

SANELE MOKGELE – SCHOOL DROPOUT
29:18 - Others got their work on WhatsApp but if you don’t have WhatsApp, you didn’t receive the work. 10:24 - ... I have failed grade 11 so that is why I decided that it’s best I just drop out of school.
VO – It wasn’t the first time Sanele had failed a grade. This time, though, the pandemic dashed any hope of bouncing back. And he’s not alone…
LINK (shot in car) - We are in Kanana Park, a poverty stricken township in the Vaal. This area has seen a massive number of students like Sanele who have decided not to go back to the classroom this year. I'm on my way to meet up with another young man in the same position.
VO – Twenty-year old Thapelo Mokgeletsane, - already battling the demands of living in aimpoverished community – struggled to adapt during the pandemic.
THAPELO MOKGELETSANE – SCHOOL DROPOUT
39:23 - .... I worked in term one and failed and I was under pressure from that moment.
VO – But Thapelo’s life altering decision doesn’t appear to have moved those untrusted whis education.
THAPELO MOKGELETSANE – SCHOOL DROPOUT
CLAIRE - 45:50 - Did the school call you to find out if you’re coming back to school this year? THAPELO – 46:54 - No. Only my friends asked. No teacher or principal. No one asked.
VO: One of more than 60% of learners in a lower grade than appropriate for their age, Thapelo’s struggles began long before Covid. And while the pandemic was the straw that broke the camel’s back, South Africa’s dropout scourge is complex.

LINK (shot in classroom) - For some students, dropping out is the
result of years of academic hardships and wrong turns. For others, the
decision is a response to conflicting life pressures - the need to help
support their family financially or the demands of caring for siblings or
their own child.
MEREL MANSFIELD – ZERO DROPOUT
A child can be pushed from school through experiences at school 10:57 Home factors and community factors that they navigate.
VO: Merle Mansfield is director of NGO Zero Dropout
MERLE MANSFIELD – ZERO DROPOUT
11:15- Now as these factors increase in your life without any protective interventions, your disengagement heightens and eventually your disengagement becomes so heightened that you completely disengage from school and drop out.
VO: In other words, dropping out isn’t the result of a single event. Instead, it’s a snowball effect of one challenge building on another - and a global pandemic has simply added more snow.

MERLE MANSFIELD – ZERO DROPOUT
12:26- So we see how the impacts of food security, job security, income within households have also been threatened. And that crisis and stress environment has impacted our kids. 12:39- So if we're looking at how those factors at both pushing and pulling kids from school, the impact of dropout is or the increase in, dropout is expected.

ELIJAH MHLANGA – DEPT OF BASIC EDUCATION
29:33 What I'm saying is that there are many efforts that have been put into supporting children, what is lacking is societal involvement.
VO: Elijah Mhlanga is spokesperson for the Department of Basic Education.
24:02 - Where are we losing the kids to when they're not in school? Where are they? Maybe that's what you also need to ask ourselves. 26:15 - Who is there? Why are those people not bringing you back to school?
VO: It seems, in attempting to answer that question, the Department sometimes opts for the stick over the carrot.
18:13 - That's why even in the South African Schools Act, ... currently it says if a person whether Caregiver, a parent or neighbor or whoever, if you're not getting a child to be in school, especially if they're official school going age, the law must take its course and in this case we said imprisonment of up to six months. 18:36 - But we are amending that to say 12 months.

VO: With 750 thousand of the country’s 13 million school-aged children not in class by May last year, it’s hard to see what impact a longer possible jail term will have. And what of people like Sanele and Thapelo?

MERLE MANSFIELD – ZERO DROPOUT
13:15 - ... our education system has a compulsory school going age, and it is from 7 to 16. 13:39 - These are learners who are often older than 16 years old so there seems to be less impetus to do something about that.
VO: The highest dropout numbers were of school pupils in grade eight and nine, followed by those in the FET phase between grade 10 and 12. The department adds that learners between 50 to 75% of a normal year’s worth of learning was lost during 2020.

LINK - When you look beyond the skyrocketing dropout rate, you'll discover personal stories of young people who are all dealing with their own challenges. They might think that dropping out is the best decision for now but what does this mean for their future and ours?

ELIJAH MHLANGA – DEPT OF BASIC EDUCATION
17:48 - We invest in them and the planning and funding allocation is
based exactly on that. 17:54- So when a child does not come to school for whatever reason, they drop out, it becomes a loss not just to the school or the system but to the country.

VO – While the Department counts the cost of an investment without a return, Thapelo and Sanele are clinging to hope of a better life. But it’s hard to ignore that they’re facing the future as statistics: two of millions not in education, not in employment, not in training.


THAPELO MOKGELETSANE – SCHOOL DROPOUT
38:13 - ... I want to go to college and learn technical skills and see what I can do because I won’t go back to normal school. 42:01 - ... I have two younger siblings and my mom is the only one working at home. I just wish to also be able to take care of them.

SANELE MOKGELE – SCHOOL DROPOUT
17:47 – ... I want to do something that will get me a job fast and a good job for me before I think about stealing because I know if I continue sitting at home I might just start thinking about doing crimes and I don't like that.
